name: 510(k), De Novo and PMA for AI Devices
blurb: Which FDA pathway an AI device takes, and why most use 510(k).
title: 510(k), De Novo and PMA for AI Devices
answer: Most AI devices are moderate risk and are cleared through the 510(k) pathway as substantially equivalent to an existing predicate. Novel moderate risk devices without a predicate use De Novo, which then creates a predicate for followers, and high risk devices need premarket approval with clinical evidence.

reading.body:
Most AI medical devices are moderate risk and reach the market through 510(k) clearance against an existing predicate, not through the harder approval routes.

The pathway follows risk class rather than the AI itself. Class II devices, which is where most clinical software that analyses images or signals sits, need 510(k) clearance showing substantial equivalence to a legally marketed predicate in intended use and technology. Class III devices need premarket approval with clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness. De Novo exists for novel low to moderate risk devices that have no predicate at all.

De Novo is the interesting case for anyone tracking how this field matures. It is slower and costlier than a 510(k), but a granted De Novo creates a new device type that later products can cite as their predicate. That makes it the mechanism by which a genuinely new AI capability becomes an ordinary one, and it explains why the pathway mix shifts over time rather than staying fixed.

The data covers the United States only. It says nothing about European routes, and the related terms point to the EU AI Act and its 2026 amendments without describing how those interact with device review. It also gives no counts, no clearance volumes, and no timing, so it establishes the structure of the pathways and not their relative traffic.

The pathway decision is made before the evidence plan exists, and it determines what evidence is even admissible. A 510(k) asks whether the new device is substantially equivalent to a predicate in intended use and technology, or whether any differences raise new safety questions. That is a comparison question, so the evidence is built around the predicate. A De Novo asks whether a novel low to moderate risk device is safe and effective on its own terms, which is why it needs more evidence and more time. A PMA asks the same question as De Novo but for high risk devices, with clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness. The three pathways are not three levels of the same test, they are three different tests.

The De Novo grant is the only one of the three that changes the market for everyone else. A 510(k) clearance consumes a predicate. A PMA approval consumes nothing that later products can cite. A De Novo grant manufactures a new device type, and every later product that cites it is a follower that never had to run the De Novo. That is why the pathway mix shifts over time: each De Novo lowers the cost of the category it creates, and the next entrant in that category faces a 510(k) instead.

For a medtech team the practical consequence is that the choice is not only about this product. A 510(k) is faster and cheaper and leaves you citing someone else's predicate. A De Novo is slower and costlier and leaves you owning the predicate others must cite. The data gives no counts, no clearance volumes, and no timing, so it establishes the structure of the pathways and not their relative traffic.

What is a predicate device?
An already marketed device that a new device is compared with to show substantial equivalence in a 510(k).

Can I talk to the FDA before submitting?
Yes, through the Q-Submission programme, including pre-submission meetings on pathway and evidence.

Why do most AI devices use 510(k) rather than De Novo or PMA?
Most AI devices are software that analyses images or signals to assist clinicians, which is a moderate risk role. Moderate risk devices usually need 510(k) clearance, so that pathway dominates.

What does a De Novo grant give a company that a 510(k) clearance does not?
A granted De Novo creates a new device type that later products can cite as a predicate. A 510(k) clearance only shows equivalence to a predicate that already exists.

Does the data say how many AI devices have gone through each pathway?
No. It cites an analysis in npj Digital Medicine finding that 510(k) cleared the vast majority of AI devices, with De Novo used for novel moderate risk products, but it gives no counts, clearance volumes, or timing.

What risk class are most AI medical devices?
The data does not assign a class to AI devices as a group. It describes Class II as moderate risk and the usual home of clinical software that analyses images or signals, and says most AI devices sit in that moderate risk role.

Does this apply outside the United States?
No. The data covers the United States only and says nothing about European routes.

explainer:
The FDA classifies devices by risk. Class I devices are low risk and mostly exempt from premarket review. Class II devices are moderate risk and usually need 510(k) clearance, which requires showing the new device is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate in intended use and technology, or that differences do not raise new safety questions. Class III devices are high risk and need premarket approval, the most demanding pathway, with clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness.

De Novo classification fills the gap for novel devices of low to moderate risk that have no predicate. It is slower and needs more evidence than a 510(k), but once granted it creates a new device type that later products can cite as a predicate. Most AI devices are software that analyses images or signals to assist clinicians, a moderate risk role, which is why 510(k) dominates. Choosing a pathway early shapes the whole evidence plan, and the FDA's pre-submission programme lets makers discuss it with the agency first.

The three routes

A medical device reaches the US market through one of three pathways depending on its risk and novelty. The 510(k) route shows that a device is substantially equivalent to one already on the market, and it is by far the most common for AI devices. The De Novo route is for novel low to moderate risk devices with no equivalent, and it creates a new device type that later devices can then cite. Premarket approval is for the highest risk devices and requires clinical evidence that the device is safe and effective; few AI devices have taken it.

What the choice depends on

For an AI device, the central question is whether a legally marketed predicate exists with the same intended use and similar technology. Because many AI imaging devices now exist, most new ones can find a predicate, which is why 510(k) dominates. A device that does something new, such as a diagnosis without clinician review in a new setting, needs De Novo. A device whose failure could cause serious harm, or that makes a treatment decision, may need premarket approval regardless of novelty.

What AI adds to each pathway

Whichever route, the submission has to describe the model, its training and test data, its performance across patient groups and its limitations. Manufacturers that expect to update the model can include a predetermined change control plan describing what changes they intend and how they will validate them, which lets updates proceed without a new submission for each. The agency has issued guidance on that and on the content of AI device submissions, and the plan has become a standard part of submissions for devices that learn or are frequently retrained.
